# Policy brief: sharing revenue and cost risk with a rail operator

<!-- Generated by scripts/build_docs.py from results/*.json and data/facts.csv. Edit docs/templates/policy_brief.md instead. -->

*Independent desk study on public information, built with AI assistance. Not affiliated with or endorsed by any
authority, operator or government. The model is stylised and its contract terms are illustrative. Author: Wenjie
Luo (GitHub LUOaini1213). Fact numbers (F01 and so on) refer to [fact_base.md](fact_base.md).*

## Issue

When an operator is appointed for a new line, the contract decides who carries three risks: how many people ride,
what it costs to run, and how quickly fares follow costs. The same question appears in a different form for a
cross-border line where the operator sets the fare. This note sets out the options and what each one trades away.
It does not recommend one.

## Background from the public record

- Singapore has used more than one form. Under the New Rail Financing Framework (NRFF) the operator keeps fares
  and pays a licence charge (F02). Version one had no sharing of a fare-revenue shortfall (F03); version two shares
  part of a shortfall and takes more of the profit in good years (F04, F05). LTA labels the operator's commercial
  risk High / Medium across the two versions.
- For new lines the Government has kept fare revenue and paid a service fee: the Thomson-East Coast Line (F17),
  and the Jurong Region Line, awarded for nine years plus an optional two, about S$750 million for 11 years (F22). The stated reason is uncertain ridership in the
  early years (F26). LTA has said it will review the model when the first licence expires (F30).
- The Cross Island Line was tendered on the same basis and not awarded in November 2024, because proposals "have
  not adequately reflected the uncertainties" of operating the line (F25). No later award was found (F34,
  UNVERIFIED).
- The RTS Link is different in kind: a 30-year first concession in which the operating company sets fares
  commercially and finances the operating assets (F64 to F66, F70). Service is expected in February 2027 (F72).

## Options

- **A. Net-cost concession.** Operator keeps revenue, pays a fixed charge.
- **B. Gross-cost service fee.** Authority keeps revenue, pays an indexed fee with incentives and deductions.
- **C. Hybrid.** Net-cost base; the authority shares a revenue shortfall beyond a deadband and takes a share of
  profit above set margins.
- **D. Long concession.** Operator sets fares, finances operating assets, pays the grantors.

## Analysis

A stylised line, sized on one existing line's 2025 ridership (F52), was simulated 20,000
times over 15 years. Each option was priced to give the operator the same
5% margin on the expected path, so differences come from risk and not
from price.

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Operator margin, fifth percentile | -4.2% | 0.7% | 0.8% | -4.3% |
| Operator margin, ninety-fifth percentile | 7.8% | 7.4% | 5.7% | 7.8% |
| Operator loses money over the term | 24% | 3% | 5% | 23% |
| Authority's present value, standard deviation (S$m) | 21 | 85 | 57 | 4 |
| Operator keeps, per extra dollar from ridership | 1.00 | 0.00 | 0.53 | 1.00 |

Four points follow.

1. **Risk does not disappear; it moves.** Under A the operator carries all of a ridership fall. Under B the
   authority does. Under C, with the illustrative bands, the operator carries
   47% of a steady shortfall and
   61% of a pandemic-like one.
2. **Protection costs incentive.** B removes the operator's reason to grow ridership, so effort has to be bought
   through the incentive regime; in the model one standard deviation of reliability moves
   S$20m of present value between the parties. C keeps about
   half the incentive on the expected path but only
   0.11 per dollar once the upper
   band applies.
3. **Fare lag is a contract term in disguise.** If yearly fare increases are capped at
   2% and the deferral is covered by subsidy, the authority bears
   about S$222m under A; uncovered, the operator bears
   S$233m. Under D the question does not arise,
   because the operator sets the fare, and the exposure shifts to how demand responds, which the model does not
   capture.
4. **Length multiplies tail risk.** Over 30 years the assumed
   chance of at least one pandemic-like event is
   44%, and the operator in D loses money over
   the term in 33% of runs.

**Procurement.** With two illustrative bidders 8% apart on price, the cheaper
wins until quality carries more than 47% of the score. A fixed fee
4% below the calibrated level raises the chance of a loss over
an 11-year term from 3% to
19%. Evaluating quality before price, as published for
one tender (F24), is one protection; testing a bid against cost scenarios is another.

**RTS Link.** The published opening estimate of 40,000 passengers a day (F69) is
13% of Woodlands Checkpoint's daily volume (F77). No fare had been
announced when sources were checked (F66). At an illustrative S$5, yearly
revenue would be S$73m; against an illustrative yearly cost of
S$100m break-even needs
54,795 trips a day. The operator's costs are not public, so this
frames the question and does not answer it. If half of tickets were priced in ringgit, the range of exchange
rates since 2015 would move revenue between 96% and
106% of the launch level; costs in the same currency mix offset most
of that.

## Trade-offs

| Aim | Favours | Cost of pursuing it |
|---|---|---|
| Stable operator finances on a new line with unknown demand | B | Authority's budget carries demand risk; incentives must be designed and monitored |
| Strong commercial drive on a mature line | A | Operator failure risk in a downturn; renegotiation pressure |
| A middle path | C | Band design is hard to calibrate and can blunt incentives at the margins |
| No fare-setting role for the authorities, private finance of assets | D | Fare level and tail risk sit with one company for a long term; step-in and review terms matter |

## What would change the picture

- **Evidence on demand.** Once a line has a ridership record, the case for the authority holding revenue risk
  weakens; the published intention to review after the first licence (F30) fits this.
- **Cost flexibility.** If costs could be cut when ridership falls, A and D would be less exposed than modelled.
- **Demand response to fares.** For D, results depend on how travellers respond to fare levels against the
  alternatives; published benchmarks are limited to the shuttle train (F80).
- **Real terms.** Actual bands, incentive sizes, indexation and concession payments are not public. Any of them
  could move these numbers a long way.
- **Correlation.** A downturn that cuts ridership and raises costs together would make every tail worse.
